subject: SE Group presentation/Foothills update
comment: Hello Chris, Want to get a quick note to you before Dan and I leave town tomorrow for most of March. We attended the meeting at Public Lands February 22 when Tyler Fonarow presented the final report from the SE Group. We are encouraged that PL seems to have changed their paradigm of constructing trails first and foremost, no matter the cost, to now recognizing that the Foothills are vulnerable natural lands that need holistic stewardship to protect the flora and fauna, and the very nature, that the majority of recreationists want to experience. Hopefully PL will follow the recommendations of the SE Group which includes developing management and maintenance plans, collection additional user data, as well as involving a large cross-section of the community in making decisions before moving forward. Several members of the mtn bike community (who have been the most vociferous pushing the original plan which they would still like to see completed as originally planned) attended virtually. Kenton Peters (SLTrails Alliance) said it was time to cut to the chase and wanted to know when the trails on the 2020 plan were going to be built, including Twin Peaks and Dry Creek, that the obfuscating had gone on long enough. Both Tyler Fonarow and Tyler Murdock made it clear that the process recommended by the SE Group was going to be followed. PL said they are going to go before the CC in March (or April) to request the $350,000 that had originally been budgeted to build the Phase 1 trails in the 2020 Plan. They indicated at the public meeting that they will request to use the funds to initiate the processes outlined by the SE Group including developing maintenance and management plans, and setting up a Community Action Group to assist with decision making. The new PL full time ecologist said he intends to prioritize protecting the Foothills habitats, and endemic flora and fauna. Unfortunately Dan and I will not be here for the Council's March 5 or March 26 public meetings. (We will, however, be here in April.) I am sure that the mtn bike advocates will line up their HS teams to pressure the CC to promise more trails now. However we would like the CC to encourage PL to follow the SE Group recommendations to steward the Foothills holistically, including defining the needs and purposes of both existing and potentially new trails before moving forward. Anyway, just wanted to give you a heads up. If the PL presentation is on the April agenda we will be there. Thanks! And enjoy the arrival of spring. It's chilly today but the air is clear and the iconic SLC views are beautiful! Hilary

subject: UTA bus stop ID 102137
comment: Hi All, Today, it was noticed that UTA has marked the ground, presumably for this bus stop to be moved a couple of feet to the east of where the bus stop is currently located. In my opinion and the opinion of several neighbors, this is not the best solution for this stop location, as it will be located even further into our residential neighborhood, as it continues to serve LDS Hospital ED patients. We (the neighbors) have continued to experience several unstable LDS Hospital patients make their way to this bus stop location, in the past several weeks. The following is what has been reported to me, including what I have personally experienced (we have pictures and video of these incidents): On January 16th, a patient left LDS Hospital ED in a wheelchair and was followed by several security guards and hospital employees, as he eventually made his way into the middle of the road, on 7th Ave and C Street. The SLCPD were called and an ambulance responded. This patient was obviously impaired and disoriented and hospital employees did nothing to assist him, but waited for paramedics to arrive. It was unclear if this patient was attempting to access the bus, but had no other means of transportation. Neighbors who witnessed this event were saddened and concerned that these types of occurrences continue to happen. On January 17th, two biohazard bags were left on sidewalk at the bus stop location by a patient, who left LDS Hospital ED late at night. These bags were never picked up by UTA or LDS Hospital and continued to litter our neighborhood for several weeks, as nobody wanted to touch them, due to fear of contamination of infectious disease. On January 22nd, an individual (not a confirmed hospital patient) entered my backyard property and two of my neighbor's properties. When confronted, he reported he was waiting for the UTA bus. He was asked to leave several times, but continued to loiter on my property and my neighbor's property instead of waiting at the bus stop. On January 31st, a LDS Hospital ED patient camped out overnight at the bus stop located at the hospital, on 7th Avenue. They wandered around the neighborhood, knocking on doors, and asked neighbors for food and clothing. He left a sleeping bag, food, and several personal items, including medical waste at the bus stop and on the sidewalk. His waste wasn't cleaned up for several hours after neighbors reported the issue. Again, having a bus stop, that primarily serves LDS Hospital ED patients, located at a residential home with small children, in a neighborhood with small children, is not a safe or responsible decision. As UTA change day approaches, we are asking that this stop be removed or moved to hospital property, to better accommodate the people who are using it and to reduce the negative impact it is having in our neighborhood. We are proposing that UTA move this bus stop to 8th Ave and D Street, directly across the street from LDS Hospital ED, on the hospital property in front of the Avenues Surgical Center. This bus stop location will be ideally located to serve the Hospital ED patients who are leaving the ED and traveling downtown. Sincerely, Migan Lightfoot and Neighbors

subject: UofU baseball stadium land lease
comment: Since 1976, living in Yalecrest I've witnessed the following land use violations by the City Council: 1. The federal War Department's Reversionary Clause by reasoning Mt Olivet property from open space (OS) to institutional (I). 2. SLC's Riparian Overlay Ordinance by widening Red Butte Creek over 400% in miller Bird Refuge. 3. The federal Migratory Bird law by removing avian and apian habitat trees during nesting season from 2014-22. 4. The recent East Bench Master Plan developed by the community and the UofU. The Council has adopted a "benefit" analysis from Tyler Murdock that anticipates a mere 8% reduction in the left field wall by accepting $4.2 M to execute a land lease. This decision is being executed without any engineering review of cross-sections and elevations. According to Murdock, the a majority of the $4.2 M will be spent to replace existing softball and field sports facilities. He does not account for large trees, a Maxicom irrigation system, cut and excavation importation/removal, and general reclamation. Very little, if any of the $4.2 M will ever be allocated to "improvements". The damage to roadways and violations of the city's Clean Wheel Ordinance by the UofU will perpetuate if the lease is executed. A qualified hydrologist has not assessed the impact of runoff quantity and quality from artificial turf that contains carcinogens. The Council has failed to negotiate a joint use covered salt storage facility with the U as part of this process and will instead perpetuate the environmentally impactful open air storage in the Steiner Aquatic parking lot. In the final analysis, the Council will sabotage the expansion of the Salt Lake Recreation Center (Steiner) as was defined and approved by the council in the 1980's. This facility was funded by private donors and the School Board, not Salt Lake City. This us in addition to the attempt by the Council to remove open space land it does not own and prohibit use by the general public as was intended by the federal BLM. Oh and one last thought, the unprecedented commercial use (concessions, fan gear, etc.) on park open space property, tight and noise pollution, traffic and street parking impacts are further negative affronts to the surrounding community. When is enough, enough? As a registered Landscape Architect I've designed campuses, parks, riparian trails, athletic facilities and executed environmental impact assessments throughout the country along with the provision of expert witness testimony related to land use administration.

subject: Laird Heights LHD
comment: As a property owner in the Yalecrest neighborhood, I strongly support the designation of Laird Heights as a Local Historic District. I grew up at 1784 Yalecrest, attended neighborhood schools and the U, and moved to California in 1979. When I returned in 2010 to help care for my elderly mom, I was horrified by what had happened to my former neighborhood. Gigantic, incoherent McMansions had replaced a shocking number of the lovely smaller homes that my sister, many of our friends, and I grew up in. My mom, a widowed 39-year-old secretary at the U bought our house for $17,000 when I was in 5th grade. The neighborhood had many young families and a healthy mix of income levels. Salt Lake is making a mistake not to preserve old neighborhoods with smaller homes and tree-lined streets like Yalecrest. The McMansions cropping up in the neighborhood (The 1800 block of Herbert is the most egregious example) could have landed anywhere — they say nothing about this venerable 100-year-old neighborhood. I hope that my block of Yalecrest will be one of the next LHDs. Until then, I encourage you to do all in your power to respect and preserve this valuable neighborhood for another 100 years. Thank you for your consideration, J. B. Sheldon

subject: Comments for the City Council **Attachment 4 - 5 page photos
comment: Council Members: I am sending a second request today to table any action on the University of Utah baseball stadium land lease deal with the city. I just received two important documents late this afternoon (3.4.24) — that relate directly to the land deal. They raise a myriad of questions about how this deal will impact Sunnyside Park and all who use it. One is a memo from Public Lands dated March 1, 2024 and the other is the Council Staff Report dated March 5, 2024. Withholding a vote would give adequate time for the public, affected communities and stakeholders to carefully review these documents and offer feedback. This is an important step in securing public trust. Much of what has taken place with the land deal has been done privately. These documents contain new information that the public has not previously seen — including new stadium design drawings, a 20-foot setback from Guardsman Way and new proposed uses of leased land. The Council has promised that through a public engagement process, the U's $4.2 gift will be used to beautify and improve the park and create numerous public benefits. But these documents tell quite a different story suggesting that very little, if any money will be left over for park improvements, only park repairs from damage caused by the U's stadium. Here's what these city documents reveal: • It will cost $3.2 million to replace two softball fields with lights and a parking area. • It will cost $865,000 to replace the lacrosse field. These two items alone will consume most of the $4.2 million. • No community use of the ball field. A direct quote from the PL document: "The operational cost required for hourly use (of the field) will likely be prohibitive for public recreational community field reservations." Implied: The University will set such a high fee for the field's use that almost no group or individual could afford it. • A 28-foot tall baseball hitting practice building will be constructed on leased property east of the ball field. Ironically, this is adjacent to the location where the U threatened to build a 35 foot wall in left field which the city claimed would harm the park's "sightline." The City now argues that the 28-foot high building won't affect "sightline" ..... "due to a grade change" in the sloping property. As such it will only appear to be 16 feet high to a park user. If this is true, the council must do the math and realize that this same grade change would make the 35-foot wall only appear to be 23 feet high. This new information must be disclosed to the public because it invalidates the 35-foot wall argument. • Trees: The city says only 4 giant Sequoia trees will be affected by the U's new stadium. At least 20 trees surround the perimeter of the stadium. The community would like more information about how those additional 16 trees will not be affected. Also during the construction process, there are 11 trees along Guardsman Way. Because of the new 20-foot setback proposed by the U, the preservation of the Guardsman Way trees appears to be in jeopardy. If trees are lost and need replacing this is more money that will need to be subtracted from the U's $4.2 million gift. • Public bathrooms are not an additional benefit to the park since the U was going to build them anyway as part of the stadium plan. Suggesting that it will cost the U an additional $500,000 to build bathrooms gets lost in their $35 million proposed stadium. Collegiate baseball stadiums have bathrooms. • Suggestions that the softball fields and lacrosse field, which will be lost because of the stadium construction, could be paid for with City funds is highly speculative. Unless the city can immediately identify, earmark and set aside city funds for this purpose it seems doubtful funds will be found — especially within the 3-year park renovation timeframe. Sales tax receipts are reportedly down about $3 million and each month, new budget amendments — seeking tens of millions of additional dollars — are presented to the Council for approval. The heady days of ARPA money are disappearing. How realistic is it that the city would step in and commit millions to Sunnyside Park? • It is a false claim that the community would get "additional programing that brings people out for art, events, programs, recreation and community" simply because the U is building a stadium in Sunnyside park. Why does the community have to wait to receive these benefits unless a stadium is built? • Another unsubstantiated claim — that the public could use University property for recreational purposes because of this stated obstacle: "provided the University agrees...." Please be aware that from the start, the U placed a No Trespassing sign on the existing practice field and has made NO attempt to share the field for recreational purposes. Another broken promise to the community. • Impact fees that would be charged to youth athletic leagues or the public to "free up funds from the University to use toward replacing the softball fields." What hasn't been disclosed: • No light towers appear on the design concept. It's our understanding that a regulation, NCAA collegiate baseball stadium typically has 10 light towers with a foot-candle power (intensity) of 70-75. Contrast these intense stadium lights with other public lighting: 10-25 foot-candle at highway intersections, 1-2 foot-candle in residential areas, 5-10 foot candle in commercial areas. The U promised residents there wouldn't be bright lights at the stadium, yet the U is under obligation to follow NCAA standards. Please have the U disclose the foot-candle (intensity) of their stadium lights, how many they will construct, the height of the towers and where the towers will be placed. See the attached NCAA lighting document. • How much fill will the U need to create the fan-friendly berm beyond the official baseball field — and what will be the height of the concrete retaining wall needed to secure the fill? Note the photo of the berm at Smith's Park. It's about 15 -20 feet long. Does the city have the dimensions of the U's berm? They should be disclosed to this public. The new, proposed fan-friendly berm is near a cluster of mature shade trees in Sunnyside Park and would be located beyond the current practice field. How will the U avoid damaging or removing the trees? The photos below show the existing practice field wall and fence. Now visualize a new 15-20 foot berm beyond that. The steep slope is where fill must be added to create the berm — unless the U can show a different design plan. We strongly believe the trees in these photos will be affected by the new berm. A retaining wall 15-20 feet beyond the existing practice field wall will also cut into an existing soccer field. • Once the U strips land from the softball field and lacrosse field on the east side — which is about 12 feet higher than the practice field— a new retaining wall will need to be built to hold back whatever land remains after those parcels are removed. How will that affect the park's appearance and its use? • Where are the engineering studies? • Where are the environmental studies? • Where are the flood plain studies? • How much of the $4.2 million will be used to relocate irrigation lines and other infrastructure disrupted by the stadium? • Bottom line: the public won't really be asked during a public engagement period about how to spend $4.2 million on Sunnyside Park, because most of the money will be spent on reclamation projects. The promise that granting the U rights to build a stadium will enhance Sunnyside Park is untrue. The City has failed to make a compelling case for public benefits. And the University's promise to "preserving the rich legacy of Sunnyside Park for generations to come" rings hollow. Respectfully, Janet (Jan) Hemming Chair Yalecrest Neighborhood Council

subject: Comments for the City Council
comment: Jessica Wade, BLM Salt Lake City Field Manager Copy to SLC Council Members As chair of the Yalecrest Neighborhood Council it has been brought to my attention that a section of land involved in a proposed land lease deal between the City of Salt Lake and the University of Utah is under the control of the Department of Interior, Bureau of Land Management (Source: BLM land patent #43-90-0014, signed February 16, 1990, pursuant to the original Act of June 14, 1926). With your authority as Salt Lake Field Office Manager, Bureau of Land Management, I am asking you to make an immediate request to the Salt Lake City Council to table and suspend any action on this land lease. Your intervention is time sensitive since the Council is expected to vote on this tomorrow, Tuesday, March 5 at its 7 p.m. formal meeting. The suspension – preferably 90 days – would allow you to initiate a joint convening process with the Yalecrest Community – which borders Sunnyside Park and the proposed land lease property – and other stakeholders (city and university) to understand how the loss of this land could trigger social, environmental and recreational impacts. Thus far, neither the city nor the U have sufficiently demonstrated how this land transfer is in the public interest and or offers real public benefits. For 40 years, the Yalecrest community has played a leading role in shaping what is now called the Salt Lake City Sports Complex – which includes a portion of the BLM petition land the city wants to lease. Community leaders like Kimball and Laurel Young, James and Maryann Webster, Betsy Hunt, Bob Bridge, Steve Lowe and Ramone Johnson raised millions in private money so the Sports Complex could be built on the petitioned land. The pool is called the Steiner Aquatic Center in honor of Bob Steiner's generous donation. The Complex used to represent the best of public-private partnership. That partnership is now under assault. To ignore the contributions and opinions of these loyal residents and others in assisting the BLM to fulfill its legal and protective stewardship over these recreational lands would discredit and dishonor their tireless and faithful service as well as hundreds of nearby residents who will be significantly impacted. Respectfully, Janet (Jan) Hemming Chair Yalecrest Neighborhood Council

Onward, cindy c._______ From: cindy cromer <[redacted-email]> Sent: Monday, February 12, 2024 9:03 AM To: Chris Wharton <[redacted-email]>; Petro-Eschler, Victoria <[redacted-email]>; Mano, Darin <[redacted-email]>; [redacted-email] <[redacted-email]>; Eva [redacted-email]> <[redacted-email]>; [redacted-email] <[redacted-email]> Cc: Fultmer, Brian <[redacted-email]>; [redacted-email] <[redacted-email]>; lex.traughber <[redacted-email]>; Council Comments <[redacted-email]>; Lindquist, Kelsey <[redacted-email]>; Thompson, Amy <[redacted-email]> Subject: Fw: your discussion of Laird Hts. on 2/6 Dear Council Members, I had planned to make a comment at your Formal Meeting last Tuesday, but the queue was so long that the most constructive thing I could do in the moment was to shorten your meeting by 2 minutes by leaving. Here is the comment I had planned to make, updated with some helpful information from Lex Traughber and Kelsey Lindquist in Planning. Comment to the City Council, drafted for 2/6 From Cindy Cromer Re proposal for Laird Hts. Historic District Last week I talked to the Landmarks Commission about how the Planning Commission had chosen to ignore the ordinance and send a negative recommendation regarding the proposed Laird Heights Historic District. You did not focus on the Planning Commission ill-conceived advice in your Work Session on 2/6, to my relief. You did focus on the requirements for new construction in historic districts. The big problem is with large multiple unit apartment buildings where the base zoning is not compatible with the historic overlay. This problem occurs frequently in the Central City District. But in Laird Heights, there are few noncontributory buildings which present opportunities for new construction of primary dwellings. There are only 2 vacant parcels. The proposed district is so important precisely because of the concentration of contributory structures. There are not many opportunities for new construction except as additions and ADUs. Here's the math: 66 primary dwellings with 3 which have become noncontributory since the survey in 2005. There are 2 vacant parcels (see the attachment), one of them clearly not buildable and the other unlikely to have a primary dwelling. * With the recent reinvestment in the 3 buildings which have become noncontributory and would, in an historic district, be eligible for demolition, I see almost no opportunity for new construction in the proposed district except as additions and ADUs. Even if there were opportunities for new construction in the proposed district, we have fabulous examples of infill in the Central City, Avenues, Capitol Hill, and University Historic Districts. subject: call for an immediate ceasefire now
comment: I write to you as a constituent and with Amnesty International USA with deep concern over the escalating genocide in Gaza. The U.S. government – including at the local level – is uniquely positioned to have tremendous impact in this genocide to ensure the protection of civilians and prevent further suffering by calling for an immediate and permanent ceasefire and divesting from funding Israel. Since October 7, we have witnessed genocide unfolding on an unimaginable scale in the Occupied Palestinian Territories. More than 2 million Palestinians in the occupied Gaza Strip are struggling to survive amid the Israeli military's ongoing genocidal offensive, and the level of civilian casualties has been unprecedented. This morning alone (2/29) at least 77 people (probably many more) were gunned down by IOF tanks as they tried to receive flour from aid trucks to feed their starving families. They risked death for the flour because their families are dying of starvation. I am encouraging you to publicly call for an immediate ceasefire and appeal to the Israeli government to allow life-saving fuel, water, and food into Gaza. It's literally the least you can do. The majority of Americans support a ceasefire, but President Biden has yet to call for one. In response, towns and cities across the country are rising up to pass their own resolutions. I ask that you, in your capacity, do what you can to help to pass one here. The need for an immediate ceasefire by all parties is more urgent than ever to protect civilians, prevent a mounting civilian death toll in Gaza, prevent further displacement of Palestinians, and provide an opportunity to secure the safe release of the remaining hostages. Thank you for your consideration. Sincerely, Janiece Murray
